source.title: Predicting the Impact of Data Poisoning Attacks in Blockchain-Enabled Supply Chain Networks
source.authors: U. Butt; Osama Hussien; Krison Hasanaj; Khaled Shaalan; Bilal Hassan; Haider M. Al-Khateeb

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text contains the full 22-page article.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results after partial random label flipping, showing reduced neural-network performance. It does not test fitting completely random labels or the full noise-fraction trend in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests clean versus label-flipped training data and reports neural-network classification metrics. It does not report a neural-network training error for random labels; its reported neural-network training and validation accuracy curves are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study measures intrusion-classification performance after partial label poisoning. It does not establish memorization of corrupted labels, perfect poisoned-training fit, or a test-error trend across corruption fractions. The F1 decreases alone do not test V4, and the text's unspecified changes in training accuracy cannot establish or refute it.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion that poisoning compromises intrusion-detection performance and their reported slight neural-network F1 decreases. However, their broader assertion that random flipping lowers every model's performance conflicts with Tables 2–3, where logistic regression, SVC, and XGBoost accuracy and F1 increase.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates poisoning effects in a network-intrusion task using KDDCUP’99 and an eight-layer feedforward neural network; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports results for clean data, random label flipping, and distance-based label flipping, but does not report a sweep over corruption fractions for the neural network.

fits_no_version.finding: After random label flipping, the neural network's normal-class F1 decreases from 0.86 to 0.84 and attack-class F1 from 0.87 to 0.85.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partial random label poisoning can slightly reduce a neural intrusion detector's classification F1 on KDDCUP’99.

record.problems: The neural-network comparison reports F1 Scores but not numerical training error on the poisoned data. The label-flipping rate for the neural-network comparison is not stated in that subsection. Training and validation accuracy curves are presented only as figures without numerical values in the text. The paper's descriptions of the random label-flipping rate differ: the abstract says 20% randomness, while Section 4.4 says probability 0.1.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible neural-network result rows were extracted. The clean neural-network accuracy (training 0.994, validation 0.9936, test 0.866) is not a label-noise outcome. Classical-model metrics in Tables 2–4 concern other model subjects.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit under label corruption and steadily increasing test error across corruption fractions toward complete randomization.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on memorization and generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the extracted V4 limits_scope verdict: failure to measure perfect training fit or a corruption-fraction trend is untested coverage, not evidence limiting the claim. Poisoned-training curves are unavailable as readable plots in the supplied text; their captions and qualitative discussion do not establish a final training-error value. The paper reports both 20% randomness and a flipping probability of 0.1, and uses early stopping.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test completely random labeling or report whether the network reaches zero or near-zero training error or chance test error under that condition.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed across label-corruption fractions is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The study tests a clean condition and a label-flipped condition, but does not report the neural network's training error numerically or sweep corruption fractions toward all labels being random. Its neural-network training and validation accuracy curves are figure-only.
No comparison of explicit regularization or data augmentation settings is reported.
No evidence about the order in which real patterns and noisy labels are learned is reported.
